title: Scalability Fundamentals
summary: Vertical vs horizontal scaling, statelessness, and the AKF scale cube — the base vocabulary you need before any system-design conversation.

slides.markdown:
Scaling means handling more load — more users, more data, more requests per second — without the system falling over or getting prohibitively expensive. Every system-design interview question is secretly asking: **how does this scale?**

Think of it like a restaurant: you can hire faster cooks (vertical scaling) or open more kitchens (horizontal scaling). This topic gives you the vocabulary — vertical vs horizontal, statelessness, the scale cube — that every other system-design topic builds on.

slides.sectionTitle: What "scale" actually means in an interview
slides.markdown:
When an interviewer says "scale this to 10x traffic," they rarely mean literally buying a bigger machine — they're asking whether your **architecture** can grow without a rewrite.

**Scale** has three dimensions that matter here: request volume (more QPS), data volume (more rows, more bytes), and complexity (more features, more teams touching the system). Conflating them is a common early mistake — a system that handles 10x traffic gracefully might still fall over at 10x data if its indexes were sized for the old volume.

The takeaway: before proposing a fix, name which dimension is actually growing.

slides.sectionTitle: Vertical scaling: how far it gets you, and where it breaks
slides.markdown:
**Vertical scaling** (scale-up) means giving one machine more resources — more CPU, RAM, faster disks. It's the simplest lever: no code changes, no distributed-systems complexity, just a bigger box.

It gets you surprisingly far — a single well-tuned Postgres instance on a 96-core, 768GB machine can serve tens of thousands of queries per second. But it has a hard ceiling: the biggest cloud instance available caps out, and it stays a single point of failure — if that one machine dies, everything is down.

Interview signal: propose vertical scaling first for simplicity, then explain exactly where it breaks for this problem's numbers.

slides.sectionTitle: Horizontal scaling: the shift to many small nodes
slides.markdown:
**Horizontal scaling** (scale-out) means adding more machines instead of a bigger one, spreading load across them with a load balancer. Instead of one server handling 10,000 requests/sec, ten servers each handle 1,000.

It trades simplicity for a near-unlimited ceiling: you keep adding commodity nodes as traffic grows, and losing one node doesn't take down the whole service. The cost is complexity — now you need a load balancer, service discovery, and a way to handle a request landing on any node.

That last requirement — any node can handle any request — is why statelessness (next slides) becomes non-negotiable once you scale out.

![Scale up versus scale out](assets/scale-up-vs-scale-out.svg)

Scale-up replaces one machine with a bigger one; scale-out keeps machines the same size and adds more of them behind a load balancer.

The practical difference shows up under failure: lose the one scaled-up machine and you're down entirely; lose one of ten scaled-out machines and you're still at roughly 90% capacity.

assets.alt: Scale up versus scale out comparison

slides.sectionTitle: Statelessness: why it's the precondition for horizontal scaling
slides.markdown:
A server is **stateless** if it keeps no request-specific data in memory between requests — session info, shopping carts, uploaded file chunks all live somewhere else (a database, a cache, object storage), not in the process's RAM.

This matters because horizontal scaling assumes any node can serve any request. If a server stores your session in local memory, only *that* server can serve you next — the load balancer can't freely route around it, and losing that node loses your session.

Statelessness is the precondition, not a nice-to-have: without it, adding nodes doesn't add capacity, it adds servers that only some users can actually use.

slides.sectionTitle: Sharing state without sharing memory: sessions, sticky routing, external state stores
slides.markdown:
If servers can't hold state, where does it go? Three common answers. **Sticky sessions** pin a user to one server via the load balancer — simple, but it reintroduces the fragility statelessness was meant to avoid (that server's loss still drops those sessions). **External state stores** — Redis, Memcached, a database — hold session data outside any app server, so any node can fetch it. **Client-side state** pushes it further, into a signed cookie or JWT the client resends every request.

Most production systems at scale default to external stores: the app tier stays stateless and disposable, and the state store becomes the thing you scale and replicate carefully.

slides.sectionTitle: The scale cube: x/y/z axes of scaling (AKF)
slides.markdown:
![The scale cube: x, y, and z axes](assets/scale-cube.svg)

The **AKF scale cube** names three independent ways to scale. **X-axis** — clone the whole app behind a load balancer (horizontal duplication). **Y-axis** — split by function or service (checkout, search, and auth become separate deployables). **Z-axis** — split by data (shard users A-M on one database, N-Z on another).

Most real systems combine all three. Naming which axis you're using signals you understand scaling as more than "add more servers."

assets.alt: The scale cube: x, y, and z axes

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: scaling the app tier vs scaling the data tier
slides.markdown:
The app tier and the data tier scale differently, and conflating them is a common interview stumble.

| | App tier | Data tier |
|---|---|---|
| Statelessness | Usually stateless — easy to clone | Inherently stateful — the data has to live somewhere |
| Scaling method | X-axis: add identical nodes behind a LB | Sharding (Z-axis), read replicas, partitioning |
| Bottleneck | CPU/memory per request | Disk I/O, lock contention, replication lag |
| Typical ceiling | Near-linear — add nodes, get proportional capacity | Sub-linear — cross-shard queries and rebalancing cost grow |

**How to decide:** check which tier is actually saturated (CPU on app servers vs disk I/O on the DB) before scaling either — scaling the wrong tier wastes budget and hides the real bottleneck.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: "just add more servers" without removing the stateful bottleneck
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We're slow under load — let's just add more app servers."

**Why it's wrong:** if the app servers are stateless and the real bottleneck is the single database they all share, adding app servers just means more clients hammering the same saturated database — throughput doesn't improve, and latency can get worse from added connection overhead.

**Correct model:** identify the actual bottleneck first (often the stateful tier — a database, a cache, a queue) before scaling the stateless tier around it. "Add more servers" only helps the tier that's actually out of capacity.
